turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mr Hale. I'm Niamh, one of the nurses. If you'd like to pop through, I'll get your observations done before the doctor calls you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning. Thank you, that is most kind. I am rather slow on this foot, I am afraid.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll bring the stick, Mr Hale. We were stuck in that waiting room a good while.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): No hurry. Arm out for me, please. Blood pressure is a hundred and fifty-two over eighty-eight, and your pulse is seventy-six, nice and steady.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that satisfactory? I did try to keep quite still.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): A touch on the high side, but the doctor will put it in context. Temperature is thirty-six point six, and your oxygen level is ninety-eight per cent.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He looked a bit flushed in the car, mind you, with the heater on full blast.
[SEG0008] person_1 (NURSE): You're all set. Doctor Okonkwo won't be long. There's water just there if you'd like it.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you very much indeed.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, Mr Hale, I'm Doctor Okonkwo. Sit wherever the foot is happiest. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. I am sorry to be a nuisance. My big toe, the right one, has become exceedingly painful and swollen. It came on last night.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): That does sound miserable. Tell me about the pain, however it comes.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): It is a throbbing, burning pain, and I could scarcely bear the sheet against it. I would call it severe. I, um, hardly slept a wink.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He was up at about three, pacing the landing, which he simply never does.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is the swelling the whole foot, or more the toe itself?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Chiefly the big toe, around the joint. It looks rather red as well, if I am any judge.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or have you felt generally off colour?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I have not felt feverish at all. Apart from the foot I feel quite myself.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Have you knocked it, or had any injury to it?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I do not believe so. There has been no injury that I can recall.
[SEG0021] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sorry, you did catch it on the chair in the kitchen yesterday evening. I heard you, which is not like you at all.

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. Yes, you are quite right, and I do apologise. I kicked the leg of the dining chair. It hurt for a moment, and then I thought nothing more of it. Well, actually, perhaps that does matter.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): It may well do. So a knock yesterday evening, then this severe pain through the night. How is it sitting here now?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Still very painful if I take any weight on it. Keeping it up on a cushion eases it a little.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Has anything like this happened before?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. The same toe, the same business, about a year back, or perhaps longer. Last winter, or the one before that, and I am afraid I cannot date it with any honesty.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I wasn't looking after him then. His daughter mentioned a bad toe once, but I couldn't tell you the month.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): And did that spell settle?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): It did, after several days. I did not trouble the surgery that time, which I rather regret.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any other joints joining in? Knees, the other ankle, your hands?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing else. It is only this one toe.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Before I forget, how was the journey in? It has been filthy weather.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Quite dreadful, Doctor. The traffic on the ring road was at a standstill. We sat by the retail park for an age.
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): A lorry had broken down on the roundabout, and then the school run piled in behind it.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I had the cricket on the wireless while we waited. England were wobbling, I thought, though I only caught the tail of the morning session.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Were they really? I haven't looked. My nephew was meant to be at a club match yesterday and the whole thing was rained off.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Same story with my grandson's football. He's seven, and he was absolutely furious. New boots, and nowhere to wear them.

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Children do feel these disappointments keenly. My own grandson is devoted to model trains, which is a calmer pursuit. We spent Sunday laying a great length of track in the spare room.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): That sounds a far better use of a wet Sunday than sitting on the ring road. Shall we come back to this foot?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course. I do apologise for wandering off.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not in the least. What medicines do you take regularly?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I take a water tablet each morning, for my blood pressure. Bendroflumethiazide. The dose is two and a half milligrams, I believe.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Mr Hale, the box at home says five milligrams. I collected it from the chemist on Tuesday, and I did check the label.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Did it say five? I may well be mistaken. I have taken one tablet each morning for years, whatever is in the box. I would not swear to the strength.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then we'll leave the exact strength until we see the box, and not guess. Do you manage it every day, or do doses get missed?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I am generally careful. I would not claim I have never forgotten, but the intention is every morning.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He missed Sunday, and Thursday last week as well. Not every week, but it isn't perfect.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): So most mornings, with the occasional miss. Anything else at all, prescribed or from the chemist?
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing else that I take regularly. I am not in the habit of painkillers.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): None that I am aware of. I have never been told that I am allergic to a drug.
[SEG0052] person_3 (CAREGIVER): His daughter once said penicillin upset him as a child. A rash, she thought. I've never seen that written down.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): I have no memory of any such thing. I was given penicillin for a chest infection some years ago, and I had no difficulty whatever. I would not call it an allergy.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then it's disputed, and I shan't rely on penicillin today either way. How about alcohol?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): I take a few beers at the weekend. Three or four pints of bitter on a Saturday, as a rule. I do not drink in the week.
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): And tobacco?
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. Not one cigarette, in all my life.
[SEG0058] person_4 (DOCTOR): May I look at the toe? I'll be as gentle as I can.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Please do. I shall do my best to keep still.

[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): The right big toe is swollen and red over the joint, and it's hot to the touch. It's exquisitely tender. The skin isn't broken, the other toes look normal, and the calf is soft and not tender.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): It is certainly sore when you press. I am sorry.
[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): You're doing brilliantly, truly. You look well in yourself, which is reassuring.

[SEG0063] person_4 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, this looks very much like an acute attack of gout. Weekend beer and a water tablet both push the uric acid up, and a knock can set it off. I can't completely set aside a simple soft-tissue injury from the chair, but gout is my working impression.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Gout. My father had gout, now you say the word. I had rather hoped it would not be that.
[SEG0065] person_4 (DOCTOR): It does run in families at times. For treatment, I'd usually start an anti-inflammatory, naproxen, five hundred milligrams twice a day with food, for a short course.
[SEG0066] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He can't have ibuprofen. Last spring, a few days of it gave him dreadful heartburn, and he brought up a bit of blood. The doctor then said no more of those tablets.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that is quite correct. I should have said. I have avoided them ever since.

[SEG0068] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that changes the plan. I will not use naproxen, or any anti-inflammatory, after a bleed like that. We'll use colchicine instead: five hundred micrograms twice a day, by mouth, for five days. If diarrhoea starts, stop it and ring the surgery.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): Five hundred micrograms, twice daily, for five days. I shall write that down carefully.

[SEG0070] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'd like a blood test for uric acid as well. It can be normal in the middle of an attack, so it won't settle the diagnosis on its own, but it's worth having, along with a kidney check because of the water tablet.
[SEG0071] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Could that be done today, while we're here?
[SEG0072] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes. The nurse can take it before you go. Consider it booked now, not something we'll only do if this drags on.
[SEG0073] person_4 (DOCTOR): While it settles, rest the foot up, and a cool flannel is fine if it soothes. And ease right off the beer this weekend, Saturday pints included.
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall do without them. It seems a modest price.

[SEG0075] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the toe is not improving in three days, or if you feel feverish or the redness starts tracking up the foot, come straight back. Otherwise I will see you in a fortnight to go through the results. Please bring the bendroflumethiazide box so we can settle the dose.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): In a fortnight, and I shall bring the box. Yes, that is perfectly clear.
[SEG0077] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll put both on the kitchen calendar when we get in.
[SEG0078] person_4 (DOCTOR): Niamh, are you free to take that blood for us?
[SEG0079] person_1 (NURSE): I am, yes. Uric acid and kidney function?
[SEG0080] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's the one. Thank you.
[SEG0081] person_1 (NURSE): Sharp scratch, Mr Hale. Both bottles are done, the uric acid and the kidney test. Press on this cotton wool for a minute.
[SEG0082] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. You have all been exceedingly kind.
[SEG0083] person_4 (DOCTOR): Look after that toe, and we'll speak in two weeks. If anything worries you before then, you are very welcome to telephone.
[SEG0084] person_2 (PATIENT): I am most grateful, Doctor. Good morning to you all.
